messages.subject: Ranef not giving values for all sites
messages.subject_clean: Ranef not giving values for all sites
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am trying to retrieve site abundance estimates for a multinomial poisson model multinomPois() with removal sampling. However, only a portion of sites are actually given estimates when I call ranef(). The rest of the sites are given 0 for the mean and mode and NA for the confidence intervals. My data consists of 3-8 survey events per site. The 3-survey sites did not capture anything and the rest have either 6 or 8 surveys. The only sites given estimates using ranef() are the sites with all 8 surveys. I have tested this model by removing the extra 2 survey events of the 8-survey sites and ranef() will give me estimates for all sites (minus the 3-survey sites - but we assume them zero anyways). It seems to be the missing survey data that is causing the problem.

Here is one of the 6-survey sites as an example of how its coded. I am also using 2 survey covariates and there are values corresponding with every survey and NAs where a survey did not.

Survey Event    1       2       3       4       5       6       7       8
Site  Counts     8       5       3       3       2       0     NA    NA

What perplexes me is that this model (and a more complicated version with abundance covariates) runs without error. I am able to predict out the model results and graph them. I can run the Nmix.gof.test() on the model just fine. It seems to just be ranef() that does not work completely. It doesn't give an error just the warning "Some observations have been discarded because corresponding covariates were missing."

Please let me know if there is a solution.

Thank you,

Jena

messages.subject: (more) publicity for the spOccupancy package
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

at the Swiss Ornithological Institute, we’re interested in producing routine species distribution maps for a large number of bird species year-round, e.g. every month, based on checklist data containing detection/nondetections. If possible, our preference would be to use some SDM that explicitly takes into account imperfect detection, i.e., some sort of occupancy model. Over the last days I have been experimenting with different model fitting functions in the spOccupancy package (https://www.jeffdoser.com/files/spoccupancy-web/) and found them to be really good.

Different types of spatial and spatio-temporal occupancy models can be fit in very reasonable time (i.e., minutes rather than hours or days as with BUGS software) to data sets with many 1000’s of sites and then I make predictions to the 42,000 km2 of the country again in just a couple of minutes. One of the latest additions to the package is spatially-varying coefficient (SVC) models, which can be fit both as a “simple” binomial GLM and as an occupancy model.

If you like occupancy models and colorful species distribution maps, then you should really check this package out. ESPECIALLY, if you have large data sets.

(And no, I don’t have any direct financial interests in the package 😊..)

Best regards  --- Marc

this is a forum for the R package unmarked, but happy to help some with PRESENCE if I can :)

OK, so to me your model looks hugely overparameterized. With just 25 sites, I would not try to fit more than about 2-3 parameters. Have you tried building up your model in increasing complexity, starting with the Null model with one intercept in occupancy and detection each ? I assume this model "runs" in the sense of giving estimates that look numerically OK ? If so, then I'd add one covariate at a time, step by step, starting with your favourite one. As soon as you get such very large or very small point estimates and/or SE estimates, you know probably are asking too much from your data set, which statistically speaking is very small (sorry ...).

Dear Pinto,

that's a classic. We ought to put the solution on some website ... Here's a sketch how to do this, based on some code I wrote just yesterday:

# Create prediction covariates on original scale in the range that you want (here, 200 - 3000 metres)
npred <- 100
x.elev.orig <- seq(200, 3000, length.out = npred)

# Now transform the prediction covariate with mean and sd as computed from the actual covariate vector, which you used in scaled manner in the model fitting
x.elev <- ( x.elev.orig - mns[1] ) / sds[1]                  # This is like scale, but with custom mean and sd

# Then, use predict() on the fitted model object, and using x.elev as the covariate for which you predict

# Finally, to plot you can simply plot the prediction AGAINST THE ORIGINAL x.elev.orig and all is fine

Hope this makes sense ...

Note that your mileage may vary with this suggestion:

> Run the model without scaling/standardizing.  If you get (essentially) the same P-values for all parameters from the model with scaling, then that tells me that scaling wasn't necessary and getting predictions with the covariates in the original scale is then straightforward.  Scaling covariates is never wrong but its effects on increasing numerical precision (i.e., minimizing computer round-off error) doesn't always result in an improvement.
>
However, if there were "unscale = TRUE" and "scalingForAllCovariates = TRUE" options in those routines for model construction, predictions, and parameter tables, that would be really great.  I would certainly contribute (small amounts of) money and beverages of choice to those programming that.

Jim

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Changing scale on plot
messages.body_plain:
You can use the scale() function inside your formulas.

Create the unmarked frame without standardizing any covariates. Then in your formula you can specify something like ~1~scale(elevation). The parameter estimates you see in the summary will be as if you standardized elevation beforehand. You can then just provide the covariate on the original scale in your newdata when using predict(), and it will be scaled automatically for you. See example below.

library(unmarked)

set.seed(1)
N <- 100
J <- 5
x <- rnorm(N, 2, 0.3)
psi <- plogis(-3 + 0.7*x)
z <- rbinom(N, 1, psi)
p <- 0.5

y <- matrix(NA, N, J)
for (i in 1:N){
  y[i,] <- rbinom(J, 1, p*z[i])
}

umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y, siteCovs=data.frame(x=x))

x_mn <- mean(x)
x_sd <- sd(x)

umf_scaled <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y, siteCovs=data.frame(x=(x-x_mn)/x_sd))

# Fit models (identical)
(mod_scaled <- occu(~1~x, umf_scaled))
(mod <- occu(~1~scale(x), umf))

# Make a range of x for plotting
range_x <- range(x)
new_x <- seq(range_x[1], range_x[2], length.out = 100)
# scale it manually
new_x_scaled <- (new_x - x_mn) / x_sd

nd <- data.frame(x = new_x)
nd_scaled <- data.frame(x = new_x_scaled)

pr_scaled <- predict(mod_scaled, 'state', newdata=nd_scaled)
pr <- predict(mod, 'state', newdata=nd)

head(pr_scaled)
head(pr)

plot(new_x, pr_scaled$Predicted, type='l')

plot(new_x, pr$Predicted, type='l')

messages.subject_clean: AIC ranking and GOF results in NB pcount models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am analyzing four years of population count data in the stacked format using pcount, with a relatively small data set (~18 sites across four years). I am comparing seven models containing different covariates to explain patterns of abundance using AIC. Initially, the models were run with a Poisson distribution, but c-hat values were high (3-9) and Nmixgof.test showed poor fits for many of the individual models (because of limited data set, we couldn’t do GOF on a global model). The models were re-run using the negative binomial mixture, which reduced c-hat (< 3), the parameter estimates seem stable with increasing K, and baseline detection probability decently high (~0.5). So, seems like the NB worked better for us. When we re-ranked models using AIC, we ended up with several competing models (delta AIC < 2) at the top. However, some of these top models still had failed GOF of fit tests (p < 0.05).

Assuming we shouldn't just ditch the analysis altogether because of failed GOF tests, my question then is whether we can use GOF as an additional criterion of support for distinguishing between top models. For example, if the top two models are < 1 different in AIC, but one GOF test fails and the other doesn’t, can we use that as evidence alongside AIC in determining which one may be a better fitting model? Given what I’ve read in this group on the fact that a failed GOF test could indicate structural problems in a model beyond overdispersion, I thought it could maybe be used in this context to find support for the best best model.

Two additional follow-ups:

1. Given we still potentially have some overdispersion based on our c-hat values, is there a further correction for negative binomial parameter estimates that needs to be applied, similar to what is done in summaryOD for Poisson models?

2. Is there any information in the Kery and Royle books or elsewhere on how to interpret/use the dispersion estimate in NB models? For instance, the alpha estimate was -1.02 and significant (p = 0.01), but I wasn't sure exactly what this means.

Any advice or useful literature suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

Hi, thank you so much to everyone who puts in (volunteers!) time to develop and maintain the `unmarked` and `ubms` packages and chat pages. I have been reading through the AHME books and google chats for a few weeks now and-- based on what I’ve read-- I think (hope) I’m analyzing our bird point count data correctly. But I would really appreciate it if I can run it by this group for confirmation and also for help with residual questions (NUMBERED QUESTIONS, IN CAPS).

The data are from long-term point count monitoring of birds in national parks. We are primarily interested in estimating long-term trend, and—if possible—also getting an estimate of annual density (with 95% CI). Each species and park will be analyzed separately.

I apologize in advance for so many questions ☹

THE DATA, IN A NUTSHELL:

·        We have 20-35 point count locations in a park. Data have been collected since 2004, but in the early years only half the points were surveyed each year, and only once in the year. Since 2019 all points have been surveyed twice each year (2nd survey within 3 weeks of first).

·        Point counts are 10 min, and birds are recorded only the first time they are detected (i.e., removal sampling). For each detection, observer records species, distance to detection (bins are 0-25, 25-50, 50-100, 100m+ ), and time-of-detection (1-min intervals for 10min).

·        Site covariate data is habitat type (e.g., forest, grass, shrub, developed). Survey event covariate data include julian date, survey start time, and wind condition.

MY APPROACH WITH GDISTREMOVAL():

·        I dropped the data collected in the 100m+ bin because I think we can’t analyze distance data with an unknown bin size.

·        I stacked years and used the two visits per year to estimate phi (temporary emigration). So for example my `yDistance` data frame is set up with a row for each site-year, and with columns: Visit1Dist1, Visit1Dist2, Visit1Dist3, Visit2Dist1, Visit2Dist2, Visit2Dist3. When a site did not have a second visit that year (like in the years before 2019), I filled those cells with `NA` to indicate missing surveys –[Q1] BUT IN THE CORRESPONDING ‘yearlySiteCovs’ I ENTERED MEAN COVARIATE VALUES FOR THOSE MISSING SURVEYS B/C gdistremoval() CANNOT HAVE NA’S FOR COVARIATES, IS THAT THE CORRECT WAY TO HANDLE THIS?

·        For  ‘yearlySiteCovs`, my rows are ordered (years stacked) like: Site1Yr2004, Site1Yr2005, Site1Yr2006…. Site1Yr2022, Site2Yr2004, Site2Yr2005… [Q2] THIS SITE-MAJOR, YEAR-MINOR ORDER SEEMS TO BE THE GENERAL RULE FOR `yearlySiteCovs`, DOES IT APPLY TO `unmarkedFrameGDR` ALSO?

·        In all models I included year (numeric, scaled) as a site covariate. I am using this estimated year coefficient as a measure of trend (bootstrap w/replacement of sites to get correct 95% CI’s). [Q3] BUT IS THERE A WAY (WITHOUT LEARNING BUGS) TO ALSO ACCOUNT FOR THE UNMODELED YEAR RANDOM EFFECT?

·        I obtained site-survey density estimates with the calculation: (lambda * phi)/area— [Q4] SHOULD I DO PARAMETRIC BOOTSTRAP (SEPARATE FROM THE NON-PARAMETRIC BOOTSTRAP MENTIONED ABOVE) TO GET A 95% CI ON THAT DENSITY ESTIMATE FOR EACH SITE-VISIT?

·        [Q5] IS IT OKAY TO USE HABITAT AS A COVARIATE ON LAMBDA AND ALSO AS A COVARIATE ON DETECTION? I have seen `unmarked` examples use the same covariate on different components of the model, but I just want to double-check it’s okay. I did staged model selection by first selecting the best-fit model for the distance function, then using that to compare models with different covariates for lambda. In many cases the model with the lowest AIC included habitat as a covariate for both lambda and distance function, but the 95% CI’s on those estimates were huge.

Thank you for taking the time to read this, and for any thoughts you may be able to provide on the above questions!

> THE CORRECT WAY TO HANDLE THIS?

That's fine, they are ignored. gdistremoval is a little too aggressive with throwing errors for missing values.

> ·        For  ‘yearlySiteCovs`, my rows are ordered (years stacked) like:

> Site1Yr2004, Site1Yr2005, Site1Yr2006…. Site1Yr2022, Site2Yr2004,
> Site2Yr2005… [Q2] THIS SITE-MAJOR, YEAR-MINOR ORDER SEEMS TO BE THE GENERAL
> RULE FOR `yearlySiteCovs`, DOES IT APPLY TO `unmarkedFrameGDR` ALSO?

yearlySiteCovs are confusingly named. In this case they would be better named periodSiteCovs or something. So it should be site-major, period-minor order, e.g. Site1Sample1, Site1Sample2, Site2Sample1, Site2Sample2, etc. Site in your case being actually a site-year.

> ·        In all models I included year (numeric, scaled) as a site

> covariate. I am using this estimated year coefficient as a measure of trend
> (bootstrap w/replacement of sites to get correct 95% CI’s). [Q3] BUT IS
> THERE A WAY (WITHOUT LEARNING BUGS) TO ALSO ACCOUNT FOR THE UNMODELED YEAR
> RANDOM EFFECT?

gdistremoval actually does support random effects using the lme4-type syntax. So you could put a year random effect on lambda. This is a very new, and relatively untested feature though so be cautious.

> ·        I obtained site-survey density estimates with the calculation:

> (lambda * phi)/area— [Q4] SHOULD I DO PARAMETRIC BOOTSTRAP (SEPARATE FROM
> THE NON-PARAMETRIC BOOTSTRAP MENTIONED ABOVE) TO GET A 95% CI ON THAT
> DENSITY ESTIMATE FOR EACH SITE-VISIT?

Not sure I understand this. If you set output = 'density' in gdistremoval() then the lambda estimates and output from predict() (including a 95% CI) will already be on the density scale. You shouldn't need to adjust with area yourself, and definitely dont need to involve phi.

> ·        [Q5] IS IT OKAY TO USE HABITAT AS A COVARIATE ON LAMBDA AND ALSO

> AS A COVARIATE ON DETECTION?

Yes, that's fine.

In general with this model, I recommend building up complexity iteratively. Try fitting the distance and removal parts separately first, with gdistsamp / gmultmix or distsamp/multinomPois. Make sure the combined version makes sense in this context. In simulations I have found it can be very hard to get a good estimate of phi unless you have a lot of data. I am somewhat skeptical with your dataset you'll be able to estimate distance p, removal p, phi, *and* a random effect.

Ken
